open.title: router.replace/push restores stale hash from initial URL on dynamic param routes (segment cache seeds hash-ful canonical URL)
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/FelixK-Witt/next-hash-restore-repro

### To Reproduce

1. `npm install && npm run build && npm run start`
2. Open `http://localhost:3000/p/123#modal` in a **new tab** (direct entry, hash in the initial URL — `/p/[id]` is a dynamic param route).
3. Click the button, which runs:

   ```js
   router.replace(pathname, { scroll: false }) // pathname === '/p/123', no hash
   ```

4. Observe the URL.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** the URL stays `/p/123#modal`. Instrumenting `history.replaceState` shows the router itself calls `replaceState(..., "/p/123#modal")` although the app passed `/p/123`. Anything keyed on the hash (e.g. modals opened via `#hash` and closed with `router.replace(pathnameWithoutHash)`) can never be closed when the page was entered directly. This is a production incident for us: users cannot close modals on deep links.

**Expected:** `replaceState(..., "/p/123")`, a hash the app removed must not be restored. This worked in Next 15.x.

Notes:

- Only **dynamic param routes** are affected. The repo contains a control case: the identical component on the static root route (`/#modal`) drops the hash correctly.
- Verified on `next@16.3.0` and `next@16.3.1-canary.3` (repo pins `canary`).
- Reproduces with both Turbopack and webpack production builds, with `next start` and with a custom server; independent of `next.config`.
- Related: #91658 (closed), but neither of its linked fixes covers this path: #94144 (shipped in 16.3.0) fixes the search-param variant only, and #91670 (open) changes href resolution in `dispatchNavigateAction`, where the dispatched URL is already hash-less, that is not where the hash comes back.

### Root cause analysis

[`discoverKnownRoute`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0/packages/next/src/client/components/segment-cache/optimistic-routes.ts#L203-L215) takes the canonical URL to store on the route cache entry. It has two call sites, and they disagree about whether that URL may contain a hash.

**1. The navigation call site strips the hash, and documents why** — [`segment-cache/navigation.ts#L528-L541`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0/packages/next/src/client/components/segment-cache/navigation.ts#L528-L541):

```ts
discoverKnownRoute(
  ...
  // Store a hashless canonical URL: the entry is shared across hashes, and
  // a later same-route hash nav appends `url.hash` to it.
  createHrefFromUrl(canonicalUrl, false),
  ...
)
```

**2. The initial-load call site does not** — [`router-reducer/create-initial-router-state.ts#L107-L119`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0/packages/next/src/client/components/router-reducer/create-initial-router-state.ts#L107-L119):

```ts
discoverKnownRoute(
  ...
  canonicalUrl, // <- includes location.hash
  ...
)
```

That `canonicalUrl` is derived a few lines above at [`#L66-L72`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0/packages/next/src/client/components/router-reducer/create-initial-router-state.ts#L66-L72) as `createHrefFromUrl(location)`, and [`createHrefFromUrl`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0/packages/next/src/client/components/router-reducer/create-href-from-url.ts#L1-L6) includes the hash unless `includeHash` is explicitly `false`.

So entering `/p/123#modal` directly seeds the route cache entry with `"/p/123#modal"`. A later same-route navigation then rebuilds the target URL at [`segment-cache/navigation.ts#L398`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0/packages/next/src/client/components/segment-cache/navigation.ts#L398):

```ts
const canonicalUrl = route.canonicalUrl + url.hash
```

With the poisoned seed this yields `"/p/123#modal"` even though the dispatched `url.hash` is empty, and that string is what reaches `history.replaceState`.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 23.6.0: Mon Jul 29 21:14:30 PDT 2024; root:xnu-10063.141.2~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6000
  Available memory (MB): 32768
  Available CPU cores: 10
Binaries:
  Node: 24.12.0
  npm: 11.6.2
  Yarn: 1.22.22
  pnpm: 10.29.2
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.3.1-canary.3 // Latest available version is detected (16.3.1-canary.3).
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.2.8
  react-dom: 19.2.8
  typescript: 5.9.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Linking and Navigating

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

### Additional context

open.title: Next 16.3 regression: htmlLimitedBots matching browser UAs makes cacheable PPR pages private/no-store
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/mdotk/next-163-html-limited-cache-repro

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the public reproduction repository.
2. Run `npm install`.
3. Run `npm run build`.
4. Run `npm start`.
5. In another terminal, run `npm run check`.
6. Observe the two requests made without a user agent, with a Chrome user agent, and with a Googlebot user agent.
7. Change only the `next` dependency from 16.3.0 to 16.2.11, reinstall, rebuild, and repeat the check.

The reproduction uses:

```js
const nextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  htmlLimitedBots: /.*/,
}
```

It contains a dynamic route with a partial `generateStaticParams` result, cached route data using `"use cache"` and `cacheLife("minutes")`, and cached asynchronous metadata.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

The on-demand PPR route behaves as follows:

| Request | Next 16.2.11 | Next 16.3.0 | Next 16.3.1-canary.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No `User-Agent` | `s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=3540`; cache HIT | `s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=3540`; cache HIT | `s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=3540`; cache HIT |
| Chrome | `s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=3540`; cache HIT | **`private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`** | **`private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`** |
| Googlebot | private/no-store | private/no-store | private/no-store |

All requests return HTTP 200 with the route-specific title in the initial `<head>`. No metadata-boundary or hydration error is emitted on 16.3.

The current behavior makes every non-empty user agent matched by the custom pattern force a dynamic/non-SSG response. Ordinary browser traffic therefore loses the route's public cache policy.

Expected behavior:

- An otherwise cacheable PPR route should retain its public cache policy for ordinary browser requests.
- Matching HTML-limited agents should receive complete critical metadata in the initial head.
- The prerender and resume metadata trees should remain compatible.
- No metadata-boundary or client-render fallback should occur.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin 25.5.0
  Available memory (MB): 24576
  Available CPU cores: 12
Binaries:
  Node: 20.20.2
  npm: 10.9.2
  Yarn: N/A
  pnpm: N/A
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.3.0
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.2.3
  react-dom: 19.2.3
  typescript: N/A
Next.js Config:
  cacheComponents: true
  htmlLimitedBots: /.*/
```

The result was also reproduced on `next@16.3.1-canary.0`.

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

- cacheComponents
- Dynamic Routes
- Metadata
- Partial Prerendering (PPR)
- Performance
- Runtime
- Use Cache

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

- next build (local)
- next start (local)

### Additional context

The behavior appears to come from the combined changes in #96364 and #96367.

The 16.3 App Page runtime effectively selects:

```js
const serveStreamingMetadata =
  !userAgent ? true : shouldServeStreamingMetadata(...)

const shouldForceDynamicPPRRender =
  isRoutePPREnabled && !serveStreamingMetadata

const isSSG =
  (prerenderManifestEntry || staticPath) &&
  !shouldForceDynamicPPRRender
```

The build also converts the configured `htmlLimitedBots` regex into a user-agent `experimentalBypassFor` rule.

For `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/`:

1. Every non-empty user agent disables streaming metadata.
2. Every matched PPR request sets `shouldForceDynamicPPRRender`.
3. The request is no longer treated as SSG/prerender-cache eligible.
4. The response reaches the `revalidate: 0` path.
5. `getCacheControlHeader({ revalidate: 0 })` emits `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`.

This explains why no-UA remains cacheable while every non-empty user agent does not.

The change in #96364 prevents a blocking-metadata request from resuming a prerender tree created with the incompatible streaming-metadata shape. Simply restoring the previous `isSSG` behavior could therefore reintroduce the metadata-tree mismatch.

A durable fix likely needs to separate blocking-metadata selection from unconditional prerender-cache bypass, gate the bypass on whether route metadata is actually postponed or incompatible with the cached shell, or expose independent controls for these decisions.

Related work:

- #93401 — original custom `htmlLimitedBots` PPR metadata mismatch
- #94630 — resume metadata-tree compatibility approach
- #95406 — custom-only bot mismatch and missing metadata on 16.2
- #96364 — force dynamic PPR render for configured HTML bots
- #96367 — configured `htmlLimitedBots` cache-components bypass
- #96584 — substring semantics for generated bypass rules; does not change the `/.*/` case
- #96593 — previous report automatically closed because it lacked the now-published reproduction link

On a CDN configured to respect origin cache headers, this behavior prevents ordinary browser responses from converging to edge cache HITs. On high-cardinality public sites that can materially increase origin traffic, rendering concurrency, and memory pressure.

3. Run `pnpm nx build my-app` or cd into `apps/my-app` and run `pnpm next build` or `pnpm next dev`

### Current vs. Expected behavior

I have an Nx monorepo that follows a [single version policy](https://nx.dev/docs/concepts/decisions/dependency-management#single-version-policy), and has many Next.js applications. Each of those use the `typescript.ignoreBuildErrors` next config option, running typechecking as a separate process from the build.

This has been working with TypeScript 7 just fine by using the alias setup that the TypeScript team recommended, aliasing the `typescript` package in the repo's root package.json to v6 and installing v7 under a different name. 

```
  "@typescript/native": "npm:typescript@^7.0.2",
  "typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6@^6.0.2",
```

With this, any packages importing from `typescript` in code find v6, and any invocations of `tsc` utilize v7.

This no longer works in Next.js 16.3. Building now fails with the error: `It looks like you're trying to use TypeScript but do not have the required package(s) installed.` It tries to automatically install it, fails to do so, then fails to build.

If I switch the `typescript` version in my root package.json to simply `^7.0.2` that goes away. But I can't do that, because it breaks many other use cases in the monorepo.

What I want is for Next.js to not do anything at all, or at least the option to do nothing at all in regards to verifying my TypeScript setup; just invoke `tsc`. I get that more basic or beginner setups might benefit from automated help verifying their dependencies, but for a complex setup it causes problems.

open.title: `@next/env`: `loadEnvConfig` with `forceReload` wipes `process.env` before reading, breaking FIFO-mounted `.env` files
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/jhb-dev/next-env-fifo-repro

### To Reproduce

1. `git clone https://github.com/jhb-dev/next-env-fifo-repro && cd next-env-fifo-repro`
2. `npm install`
3. `npm run repro`

The script creates a FIFO named `.env` that serves its contents once and empty
thereafter, as a drained pipe does. It then calls `loadEnvConfig` twice: normally,
then with `forceReload: true` — what the dev bundler does on any `.env` watcher
event.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current** — the value loads, then the forced reload deletes it:

```
1. before any load:                  SECRET=undefined
2. after initial load:               SECRET="from-secret-manager"
3. after forceReload:                SECRET=undefined
```

**Expected** — a reload that reads nothing should leave the previously-loaded
environment intact.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 24.6.0: Tue Apr 21 20:19:12 PDT 2026; root:xnu-11417.140.69.710.16~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6041
  Available memory (MB): 24576
  Available CPU cores: 14
Binaries:
  Node: 22.19.0
  npm: 10.9.3
  Yarn: N/A
  pnpm: 11.1.2
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.2.12 // Latest available version is detected (16.2.12).
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.2.8
  react-dom: 19.2.8
  typescript: 6.0.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Runtime

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next dev (local)

### Additional context

`packages/next-env/index.ts` resets `process.env` before it knows the re-read will
succeed, and swallows read failures:

```ts
replaceProcessEnv(initialEnv)   // deletes everything not in the pre-load snapshot
...
try {
  const stats = statSync(dotEnvPath)
  if (!stats.isFile() && !stats.isFIFO()) continue
  const contents = readFileSync(dotEnvPath, 'utf8')
  loadedEnvFiles.push({ path: envFile, contents, env: {} })
} catch (err) {
  if (err.code !== 'ENOENT') log.error(...)   // swallowed
}
```

`initialEnv` is snapshotted before the first load, so it holds no `.env` values.
If the re-read yields nothing, the environment is gone.

This is not FIFO-specific — any transient read failure loses the environment the
same way. But FIFOs make it reachable in normal use. #70725 added `isFIFO()` so
mounted `.env` files from secret managers (1Password, Doppler) would load, on the
premise that a pipe "otherwise acts exactly like a file". A pipe can only be
consumed once, and the watcher and reload path were not adapted:

```js
// server/lib/router-utils/setup-dev-bundler.js
if (envFiles.includes(fileName)) { if (fileChanged) { envChange = true } continue }
...
if (envChange) {
  await propagateServerField(opts, 'loadEnvConfig', [{ dev: true, forceReload: true }])
}
```

1Password [documents](https://www.1password.dev/environments/local-env-file) that
FIFO mounts emit filesystem events on open, close and read. So reading the pipe
causes the event that triggers the reload that wipes the environment and cannot
refill it. The app boots fine, then loses its environment on the first watcher
event.

**Suggested fix** — read first, swap only on success:

```ts
if (forceReload && nextLoadedEnvFiles.length === 0 && loadedEnvFiles.length > 0) {
  return { combinedEnv, parsedEnv, loadedEnvFiles }
}
replaceProcessEnv(initialEnv)
```

That alone makes FIFO-mounted `.env` files work: the first read populates, later
reads come back empty, and Next.js keeps what it has.

Reproduced on `@next/env@16.2.12`; both the `isFIFO()` acceptance and the
unconditional `replaceProcessEnv(initialEnv)` are also present on `canary`.
Versions ≤ 14.x are unaffected because FIFOs were skipped entirely.

open.title: ISR revalidation retains RSC segment data via CachedParams WeakMap (external/arrayBuffers growth, amplified on Node 22)
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/udohsolomon/nextjs-isr-leak-repro

### To Reproduce

1. `npm install && npm run build` (bare app: one `app/posts/[slug]/page.tsx` with `revalidate = 3600`, 200 params from `generateStaticParams`, ~100 KB rendered body; `instrumentation.ts` logs `process.memoryUsage()` every 5s)
2. `npm run start > server.log 2>&1 &`
3. `node drive.mjs server.log 25` - forces ISR re-renders of all 200 routes per round via the `x-prerender-revalidate` header and prints the server's memory line after each round
4. Run once under Node 22.x and once under Node 24.x (fresh server each time)

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Expected:** repeated ISR re-renders of the same routes should not accumulate memory - each re-render replaces the cached entry, and the previous render's buffers become collectable and are collected.

**Current:** external/`arrayBuffers` memory produced by revalidation renders is retained across many rounds. On Node 22 the effect is much stronger than on Node 24 for the identical workload.

Minimal repro (200 routes x 25 forced-revalidation rounds, `process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers`):

| | Node 22.22.3 | Node 24.18.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior | climbs to a **75-85 MB plateau sustained for 14 consecutive rounds** (rounds 8-21) before a single full GC drops it to 27 MB, then rebuilds | collected continuously; oscillates in a **24-42 MB band** |
| RSS | 271 -> 327 MB drift | flat ~370-383 MB |

Raw per-round numbers are committed in the repro repo (`results-node22b.txt`, `results-node24.txt`).

The magnitude scales with app size. In our real application (785 ISR routes, ~100 KB RSC payloads per page) the identical A/B held **190-240 MB under Node 22 vs 72-85 MB under Node 24**, and in production (Next 16.2.7, 736 ISR pages revalidating hourly, Node 22.19, self-hosted `next start`) it accumulated to **1.16 GB of `arrayBuffers` over ~4 days** with the JS heap steady at ~230 MB - the dominant share of container RSS.

**Heap-snapshot evidence** (V8 snapshot of the live `next start` process, Node 22): the retained Buffers are RSC `segmentData`/`flightData` bytes, and every sampled retainer chain roots through the same path:

```
Buffer (segmentData bytes)
  <- Map property:segmentData
  <- context closures
  <- property:onError Object
  <- <symbol kResourceStore> Promise        (AsyncLocalStorage store captured by the cached promise)
  <- WeakMap entry                          (CachedParams, module scope)
  <- closure createPrerenderParamsForClientSegment
     (next/dist/server/request/params.js)
```

The promise cached in the module-scope `CachedParams` WeakMap (`packages/next/src/server/request/params.ts`) captures the render's AsyncLocalStorage context; through the work store's `onError`, that roots the render's RSC segment buffers for as long as the params key object stays alive - so every revalidation adds another retained render until a full GC manages to sever what is collectable. With a typical self-hosted setup (no `--max-old-space-size`, small working heap vs the ~2 GB default ceiling), full GCs are rare enough that this accumulates for days.

Checked against 16.2.12 - the `CachedParams` path is unchanged and 16.2.8-16.2.12 contain no related fix.

### Provide environment information

```
Operating System:
  Platform: linux
  Arch: x64
  Version: WSL2 (kernel 6.6) and Debian (Railway/Nixpacks container) - both reproduce
  Available memory (MB): 31821
  Available CPU cores: 22
Binaries:
  Node: 22.22.3 (strong retention) / 24.18.0 (much weaker) - production hit it on 22.19.0
  npm: 10.9.8
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.2.12 (repro; also observed on 16.2.7 in production)
  react: 19.2.3
  react-dom: 19.2.3
  typescript: 6.0.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A (plain `next start`)
```

### Which area(s) are affected?

Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR), Runtime

### Which stage(s) are affected?

next start (local), Other (self-hosted production)

### Additional context

Workarounds that contain it for us in production: run Node 24, and set `--max-old-space-size` low enough (e.g. 768 MB for a ~230 MB heap) that full GCs run regularly, which promptly collects the collectable share of the external memory. With those two changes our frontend went from grinding to 2.2+ GB RSS over days to a flat ~0.5 GB.

open.title: Nextjs test mode issue
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/melkir/testproxy-h2-repro

### To Reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/melkir/testproxy-h2-repro
cd testproxy-h2-repro
npm install
npm test
```

`experimental.testProxy: true` in `next.config.ts` breaks any outbound `fetch()` call to a server that negotiates HTTP/2 via ALPN — virtually every modern HTTPS server. No third-party library involved; the repro is a single plain `fetch()` call. A plain HTTP (no TLS) request succeeds even with `testProxy: true` — only TLS connections that negotiate `h2` are affected.

With `testProxy: true`, the request fails:

```json
{ "error": "TypeError: fetch failed", "cause": "SocketError: other side closed" }
```

(Sometimes instead: `HTTPParserError: Response does not match the HTTP/1.1 protocol`, with a raw HTTP/2 SETTINGS frame in the response bytes. Both are symptoms of the same mismatch, not two different bugs.)

Traced the mechanism in `@mswjs/interceptors`' compiled `ClientRequest` module (vendored by Next): a global `socket-interceptor` patches `net.Socket.prototype.connect` for every outbound socket in the process (not just `http.ClientRequest` traffic, so `fetch()`/undici is included). For requests with no active test context, it reconstructs the connection as a "passthrough": opens its own real socket using TLS options copied from the original connection attempt (including its ALPN list), then replays the request onto it. That machinery assumes HTTP/1.1 framing end-to-end. When the passthrough socket negotiates `h2`, the interceptor still writes plain HTTP/1.1 text and parses the response with its own vendored HTTP/1.1 parser (`llhttp`, WASM) — confirmed directly by instrumenting the compiled interceptor to log the negotiated ALPN protocol (`h2`) and the raw bytes written to the socket (`GET /zen HTTP/1.1\r\n...`).

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** with `experimental.testProxy: true` set, any `fetch()` call made during rendering to an HTTP/2-capable host fails instead of resolving.

**Expected:** requests made outside a recognized test context should pass through once and resolve normally, regardless of what protocol the upstream negotiates.

```bash
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.4.0-canary.1
```

Testing

### Which stage(s) are affected?

open.title: Inline `"use server"` function fails when returned from file-level `"use server"` function
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/hi-ogawa/reproductions/tree/main/next-rsc-returned-nested-action

### To Reproduce

The reproduction exercises the natural composition of the two `"use server"` forms. An exported function inherits the file-level directive and returns a nested function with its own inline directive and one closure capture.

```ts
'use server'

export async function outer(prefix: string) {
  async function inner(value: string) {
    'use server'
    return `${prefix}:${value}`
  }

  return inner
}
```

The routes differ only in how the Client Component receives `outer`:

1. `/imported` imports `outer` directly into the Client Component.
2. `/prop` imports `outer` in the Server Component and passes it to the Client Component as a prop.

In both routes:

1. Select **Get inner**. The client calls `outer('captured')`, stores its return value in a ref, and displays `stored:function`.
2. Select **Call inner**. The client calls the retained function with `'client'`.

The issue is that `/prop` case succeeds but `/imported` case fails with a following error:

```
 POST /imported 200 in 8ms (next.js: 1.6ms, application-code: 7ms)
  └─ ƒ outer("captured") in 0ms app/imported/actions.ts
Error: Failed to find Server Action "609f86498f34d90b3fc12f77914ba6f5f15698574f". This request might be from an older or newer deployment.
Read more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/failed-to-find-server-action
```

Run the automated reproduction with:

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm test
```

### Current vs. Expected behavior

On `/imported`, `outer` succeeds and returns a function to the client, but invoking that returned function fails:

```text
UnrecognizedActionError: Server Action "<inner-action-id>" was not found on the server.
```

On `/prop`, the same sequence succeeds and produces:

```text
result:captured:client
```

I expected `/imported` to produce the same result. The returned value is serialized to the client as a Server Action reference, so its generated action ID should remain resolvable when the client invokes it.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
Binaries:
  Node: 24.18.1
  pnpm: 10.34.5
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.3.0-canary.106
  react: 19.2.4
  react-dom: 19.2.4
  typescript: 5.9.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Server Actions

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next dev (local), next build (local), next start (local)

### Additional context

The split result was verified in:

- Turbopack development.
- Webpack development.
- Turbopack production followed by `next start`.

[PR #62052](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/62052) added support for nested inline actions inside module-level `"use server"` files. Its example includes an exported action returning nested actions, but its coverage is at the SWC transform layer. The transform works in this reproduction; the missing piece is publication of the generated nested export for the direct Client Component import path.

open.title: Server Action POSTs to an arbitrary URL supplied by a non-Next history.pushState/replaceState call
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/FahadAlazemi/next-server-action-history-retarget

### To Reproduce

```bash
npm install && npm run build && npm start
```

1. Open <http://localhost:3000/ar/signup> (route: `app/[lang]/signup/page.tsx`, form is a client component
   using `useActionState`). Wait for hydration.
2. In the devtools console, run one line:

   ```js
   history.replaceState({}, '', '/[lang]/signup')
   ```

3. Click **Sign up**.

The repo also contains `ab-test.mjs`, an automated A/B control described below.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Expected:** the Server Action POSTs to `/ar/signup` — the page it was rendered from.

**Current:** it POSTs to `/[lang]/signup`. With the locale `proxy.ts` included in the repo (modelled on a
real app's), that 307-redirects to `/ar/[lang]/signup`; the action's `fetch` receives a 404 JSON body
instead of an RSC payload and the client throws `Error: An unexpected response was received from the
server.` The user's submission is silently lost.

Without a proxy the failure is quieter and arguably worse: `POST /[lang]/signup` returns **303** and the
action *executes*, because a literal-bracket path matches the dynamic route with `lang = "[lang]"`.

### Why this is the router and not just "the URL changed"

`ab-test.mjs` runs two arms that end with an **identical `location.href`**, differing only in whether the
`replaceState` call goes through Next's patched function (`unpatched` captures the pristine method via an
init script before Next installs its patch):

```
--- mode=patched ---                          --- mode=unpatched ---
  location.href = /[lang]/signup                location.href = /[lang]/signup   <-- identical
REQ  POST /[lang]/signup                      REQ  POST /ar/signup
RES  307 /[lang]/signup                       RES  303 /ar/signup  ct=text/x-component
REQ  POST /ar/[lang]/signup                     fetch() calls: ["/ar/signup [POST]"]
RES  404  ct=application/json                   final location.href = /ar/verify
  PAGEERROR: Error: An unexpected response...   (action ran once, clean)
  fetch() calls: ["/[lang]/signup [POST]"]
```

Same address bar, opposite POST targets. The retargeting comes from the `ACTION_RESTORE` path.

### Mechanism

Next patches `window.history.pushState` / `replaceState`. When the caller's state object lacks `__NA` /
`_N` — i.e. any non-Next caller — the caller's `url` is forwarded verbatim, unvalidated:

```js
// next/dist/client/components/app-router.js
const applyUrlFromHistoryPushReplace = (url) => {
  const href = window.location.href
  dispatchAppRouterAction({ type: ACTION_RESTORE, url: new URL(url ?? href, href), ... })
}
window.history.pushState = function pushState(data, _unused, url) {
  if (data?.__NA || data?._N) return originalPushState(data, _unused, url)
  if (url) applyUrlFromHistoryPushReplace(url)
  ...
}
```

`ACTION_RESTORE` → `completeTraverseNavigation` → `canonicalUrl: createHrefFromUrl(url)`, and the Server
Action dispatch then targets exactly that:

```js
// next/dist/client/components/router-reducer/reducers/server-action-reducer.js
const res = await fetch(state.canonicalUrl, { method: 'POST', headers, body })
```

Still present on `canary` (`server-action-reducer.ts:147`, `app-router.tsx:320`).

### Is this intended?

Partly, and I want to be upfront about it. The History API integration is documented — `pushState` /
`replaceState` syncing with `usePathname` and `useSearchParams`. But the documented example pushes a
**query string** (`window.history.pushState(null, '', '?' + params)`), and nothing states that pushing a
**path** also changes where Server Action submissions are POSTed.

`usePathname()` reflecting an external push is a read. Silently retargeting a Server Action POST to a
possibly-unrouted path is a write with side effects: it either drops the submission or executes the action
with a corrupted param. If this is working as intended, a validation or a documentation note seems
warranted — right now the failure is invisible to the application.

### Provide environment information

```
next: 16.2.12 (mechanism also present on canary)
react / react-dom: 19.2.4
node: 22.22.2
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Server Actions, Navigation, Dynamic Routes

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next start (local), Other (Deployed)

### Additional context

This was distilled from a production incident where `POST /[lang]/signup` appeared twice in access logs
during a signup/OTP flow, dropping the user's submitted one-time code and — on a third occurrence that
reached the resolved path — re-executing the action and sending an unrequested code.

**I could not identify what performed the history write in that incident**, and I am not claiming this
reproduction is that trigger. The application writes no history itself; `@vercel/analytics` does compute
the exact string `/[lang]/signup` via its `computeRoute` helper but its runtime script provably does not
patch history when the Next SDK passes a route; Sentry's route vocabulary is colon-shaped. So the trigger
remains open. What this repo demonstrates is the dispatch behaviour, which reproduces deterministically on
its own.

Earlier, less careful version of this report: #96494 (closed for lacking a reproduction; its body has since
been corrected). Possibly related: #90467, #88343 — same `state.canonicalUrl` field corrupted by other
means.

open.title: CSS module styles lost after client navigation when page CSS gains `data-n-p` after ISR revalidation
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/hshahdramafever/nextjs-bug-demo

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the reproduction repository
2. `npm install && npm run build && npm start`
3. Wait about five seconds after the build finishes (see **Additional context** — the page must be regenerated on the server after its `revalidate` window)
4. Open `http://localhost:3000/` and click **Go to second page →** — the green box is styled correctly
5. Navigate back to `http://localhost:3000/` and **reload the page** (a full document load, not the browser back button)
6. Click **Go to second page →** again

**Observe:** the box renders with its CSS module class names but no styles — no green background, no padding, and no CSS rules for `.box` in the document.

7. (Optional) Inspect `<head>` in DevTools during step 6 — the stylesheet `<link>` that was present on the home page is removed on client navigation and is not re-added; the CSS file is not re-requested

Every subsequent client navigation to `/second` stays broken. Re-running `npm run build` restores the working state; restarting `next start` alone does not.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Expected:** after ISR revalidation, client-side navigation from `/` to `/second` should render the same `Box` component with the same CSS module styles as before the home page was regenerated.

**Actual:** once `/` has been re-rendered on the server (after `revalidate` expires), client navigation to `/second` drops the shared CSS module stylesheet from the document. The component mounts with hashed class names but no matching rules. This only reproduces in a **production build** (`next build` + `next start`); `next dev` is unaffected.

A freshly built app (before the home page’s first ISR regeneration) works correctly, which makes the failure easy to miss in local testing right after deploy.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
Binaries:
  Node: 24.x (or 20.x — bug is not Node-specific)
  npm: 10.x
Relevant Packages:
  next: 15.5.18  (also reproduced on 16.3.0-canary.103 with `next build --webpack`)
  react: 18.3.1
  react-dom: 18.3.1
Next.js Config:
  output: default (not standalone)
  Pages Router only — no App Router routes
```
**Version matrix (from local testing):**

| Version | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 15.3.9 | Works |
| 15.5.18 | Broken |
| 16.3.0-canary.103 | Broken with `next build --webpack`; default Turbopack build appears unaffected |
### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Pages Router

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next start (local)

### Additional context

**App shape**

| Route | Import pattern |
| --- | --- |
| `/` (`pages/index.jsx`) | Static `import Box from '../Box'` |
| `/second` (`pages/second.jsx`) | `dynamic(import('../Box'))` |

Both pages use `getStaticProps` with `revalidate: 5` (short only so the repro does not require a long wait; in a real app with a multi-minute build, `revalidate: 30` was enough because the window had already passed by the time the server came up).

`Box.jsx` imports `Box.module.css`. Both routes share the **same CSS file hash** in the build output, and that file appears in `dynamic-css-manifest.json` because `/second` loads the component through `next/dynamic`.

**What changes on the home page after ISR revalidation**

Requesting `/` HTML twice (before and after the page is regenerated on the server), the only difference is an extra attribute on the stylesheet link:

```
first request   <link rel="stylesheet" href="/_next/static/css/<hash>.css"/>
second request  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/_next/static/css/<hash>.css" data-n-p=""/>
```

Broken client navigations line up with the second version of that HTML (stylesheet tagged `data-n-p`). On navigation to `/second`, the client-side router appears to remove that page-priority stylesheet and does not reinject or re-fetch the same CSS file for the dynamically loaded component.

**Related issues / changes**

- [#68328](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/68328) — same symptom (shared CSS lost after client navigation)
- [#72959](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/72959) — introduced `dynamic-css-manifest.json` handling for CSS loaded through `next/dynamic`; this repro’s build output includes the shared module CSS in that manifest

**Why `revalidate` matters**

The bug requires the home page to have been **re-rendered on the server** after the initial build. The revalidation countdown starts when `next build` writes the static page, not when `next start` boots. In this minimal app the build takes ~6 seconds, so `revalidate: 5` avoids a long wait; in production the build is much longer and the failure shows up immediately after deploy without a special wait.

**Real-world impact**

Any Pages Router app that:

1. Statically imports a component (and its CSS module) on one route, and
2. Loads the same component via `next/dynamic` on another route, and
3. Uses ISR/`revalidate` on the static route

…can hit missing styles on client navigation after the static route’s HTML is regenerated — e.g. a marketing/home page with static promos and a CMS-driven page that lazy-loads the same row components.

open.title: Forwarded Server Actions expose the internal origin (localhost:PORT) via headers() — breaks host-based multi-tenancy when self-hosting
open.body:
# Forwarded Server Actions expose the internal origin (`localhost:PORT`) via `headers()` — breaks host-based multi-tenancy when self-hosting

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/squaredd/next-forwarded-action-host-repro

### To Reproduce

1. Two pages and one shared server action that reads `headers()`:

```js
// app/actions.js
'use server';
import { headers } from 'next/headers';
export async function whoAmI() {
  const h = await headers();
  return {
    host: h.get('host'),
    xForwardedHost: h.get('x-forwarded-host'),
    actionWasForwarded: h.get('x-action-forwarded'),
  };
}
```

- `app/a/page.jsx` renders a client component that imports `whoAmI` → the action is bundled into `app/a/page`'s worker.
- `app/b/page.jsx` does **not** import the action.
- Both pages use `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`.

2. `next build && next start -p 4111`

3. POST the action to each page (only the URL differs):

```bash
AID=$(node -e "const m=require('./.next/server/server-reference-manifest.json');console.log(Object.keys(m.node)[0])")

# control — POST to /a (page IS in the action's worker set)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4111/a \
  -H 'Host: repro.example' -H 'Origin: http://repro.example' \
  -H 'Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8' -H "next-action: $AID" \
  --data-raw '[]'
# → {"host":"repro.example","xForwardedHost":"repro.example","actionWasForwarded":null}

# bug — same POST to /b (page is NOT in the action's worker set)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4111/b \
  -H 'Host: repro.example' -H 'Origin: http://repro.example' \
  -H 'Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8' -H "next-action: $AID" \
  --data-raw '[]'
# → {"host":"localhost:4111","xForwardedHost":"repro.example","actionWasForwarded":"1"}   HTTP 200
```

Deterministic: same result 100% of runs.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** when a Server Action POST hits a route whose page is not in the action's `workers` set, `handleAction` forwards the request to a worker that has it (`selectWorkerForForwarding`, `packages/next/src/server/app-render/action-handler.ts`). The forward is an HTTP self-fetch to `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN` — which `startServer` sets to `http://localhost:PORT` (`packages/next/src/server/lib/start-server.ts`). Inside the forwarded subrequest, `headers().get('host')` returns **`localhost:PORT`** instead of the original request's host.

**Expected:** the action should observe the original request's `Host` (or the docs should state that `host` is unreliable inside actions and `x-forwarded-host` must be used).

### Why this matters (production impact)

Any self-hosted multi-tenant app that resolves the tenant from `headers().get('host')` (a very common pattern) breaks *only* for forwarded actions, which makes it maddening to debug:

- The forward is invisible: it happens on loopback, the APM shows a POST to the **target worker's literal pathname** (e.g. `/[...slug]`, brackets included) with `Host: localhost:3000` and a duplicated `x-forwarded-for`.
- Which actions get forwarded depends on the build's static import graph vs. where the action is *actually invoked* from at runtime. Shared client components (a header search box, cards reused across routes) and intercepted/parallel routes routinely cause a POST to land on a URL whose page is not in the action's worker set.
- In our production app (9 domains, host-based tenancy) this produces a steady ~1,000 failed actions/day for real users, all `Error: Project not found: localhost:3000`.

Related but distinct: #84504 (forwarding loop, fixed by #93792 — the guard prevents a *second* forward but the first forward still rewrites the Host), #62903, #58295.

### Notes on the mechanism (from reading 16.2.2 sources)

- `createForwardedActionResponse` fetches `${__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN}${workerPathname}`; `fetch` derives `Host` from the URL, so the original `Host` header is lost (it is a forbidden header and cannot be preserved via `getForwardedHeaders`).
- `x-forwarded-host` *is* preserved and carries the original host — that is also why the CSRF origin check passes inside the subrequest (`parseHostHeader` prefers `x-forwarded-host`). So the information is available; it is `headers().get('host')` that silently changes.
- A possible fix: have the forwarded fetch set the original host into the subrequest (e.g. re-write the `host` header after `getForwardedHeaders`, or make `headers()` in forwarded actions surface the original host), or document `x-forwarded-host` as the canonical way to read the host inside Server Actions.

### Provide environment information

```
Next.js: 16.2.2 (also inspected canary sources — behavior unchanged)
Node.js: v22.22.2
OS: Linux (self-hosted, `next start` behind reverse proxies; repro is plain `next start`)
```

### Which area(s) are affected?

Server Actions

### Which stage(s) are affected?

next start (local), Other (self-hosted production)

open.title: Server Action passed as an argument fails when called after navigation
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/hi-ogawa/reproductions/tree/main/next-rsc-action-argument

### To Reproduce

The reproduction includes following two actions that are exclusively accessed through two pages through two client components:

```js
// app/a/actions.ts
'use server'

export async function actionA() {
  return 'ACTION_A_OK'
}

// app/b/actions.ts
'use server'

export async function actionB(action) {
  return `ACTION_B_OK(${await action()})`
}
```

The idea is that the client component in `/a` stashes `actionA` as client state, then after the navigation, the client component in `/b` triggers `actionB(stashedAction)`. When `actionA` is called from page `/b` in that way, it leads to an error like:

```sh
⨯ Error: Failed to find Server Action "002e999fb6c51172959666feee27cb3ccda5ce5565". This request might be from an older or newer deployment.
Read more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/failed-to-find-server-action
    at ignore-listed frames {
  digest: '370130379@E974'
}
 POST /b 500 in 149ms (next.js: 3ms, application-code: 146ms)
```

Following is a step-by-step instruction:

- Run `pnpm install` and `pnpm dev`.
- Open `/a` and select **Save action A**. This retains `actionA` in shared client runtime state.
- Navigate client-side to `/b`.
- Select **Run saved action A directly** and observe that it succeeds with `ACTION_A_OK`.
- Select **Run action B with saved action A**.
- Observe an error.

The automated reproduction is available through `pnpm test`.


### Current vs. Expected behavior

Currently, calling `actionB(savedActionA)` on page B fails while decoding the arguments, before `actionB` executes. Page B statically reaches `actionB`, but it does not statically reach the retained `actionA` reference.

I expected the valid retained reference to be decoded and passed to `actionB`, producing:

```text
ACTION_B_OK(ACTION_A_OK)
```

The reproduction includes two controls:

- Calling retained `actionA` directly after navigating to page B succeeds, which confirms that the reference remains valid and normal stale-action forwarding works.
- Calling `outerAction(innerAction)` on `/nested` succeeds when the current page statically reaches both route-local action modules, which confirms that passing a server reference as an action argument is supported in that case.


### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin

  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 25.5.0: Mon Apr 27 20:41:15 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.121.6~2/RELEASE_ARM64_T6041

open.title: Telemetry _controller is always undefined due to Promise identity loss in record(), so flushDetached's abort is a silent no-op
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/ash2228/next-promise-identity-repro

### To Reproduce

Look at Telemetry.record() in packages/next/src/telemetry/storage.ts:

``` JS
record = (_events, deferred) => {
  const prom = (deferred ? /* ... */ : this.submitRecord(_events))
    .then((value) => ({ isFulfilled: true, isRejected: false, value }))
    .catch((reason) => ({ isFulfilled: false, isRejected: true, reason }))
    .then((res) => {
      if (!deferred) {
        this.queue.delete(prom)
      }
      return res
    })

  ;(prom as any)._events = Array.isArray(_events) ? _events : [_events]
  ;(prom as any)._controller = (prom as any)._controller
  this.queue.add(prom)

  return prom
}

```
1. this.submitRecord(_events) internally creates an AbortController and returns a Promise (call it Promise A) with A._controller = postController genuinely set on it:

```JS
   // inside submitRecord()
   const postController = new AbortController()
   const res = postNextTelemetryPayload(payload, postController.signal)
   res._controller = postController
   return res
```
2. record() immediately chains .then().catch().then() off Promise A. Each of those calls returns a new Promise object  , .then()/.catch() never copy custom properties from the promise they're called on. So the final prom stored in this.queue is a distinct object (Promise D) that was never Promise A, and therefore never had _controller set on it.
3. The line (prom as any)._controller = (prom as any)._controller reads undefined off prom and assigns that same undefined back to itself. It is a no-op, there is nothing to actually copy the controller from at this point in the chain.
4. Reproduce by adding a one-line assertion anywhere record() is called in dev mode: console.log((await telemetry.record(event))._controller) will print undefined every time, confirming the controller is never actually reachable through the object stored in this.queue.
Consequently, in flushDetached():
``` JS
   this.queue.forEach((item) => {
     try {
       item._controller?.abort()
       allEvents.push(...item._events)
     } catch (_) {}
   })
```
item._controller is always undefined, so item._controller?.abort() silently no-ops on every call, the optional chaining swallows this without any error or warning.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

Current behavior

Telemetry.record() chains .then().catch().then() onto the Promise returned by submitRecord(), and stores the final chained Promise in this.queue:

```js
const prom = this.submitRecord(_events)
  .then((value) => ({ isFulfilled: true, isRejected: false, value }))
  .catch((reason) => ({ isFulfilled: false, isRejected: true, reason }))
  .then((res) => { /* ... */ return res })

;(prom as any)._controller = (prom as any)._controller  // no-op, always undefined
this.queue.add(prom)
```
.then() or .catch() always return a new Promise object and never copy custom properties forward, so prom is never the same object as the Promise submitRecord() returned, the one that actually had _controller set on it. As a result, _controller is undefined on every item in this.queue.

This means flushDetached()'s cancellation logic silently does nothing:
```js
this.queue.forEach((item) => {
  try {
    item._controller?.abort()   // always a no-op, item._controller is always undefined
    allEvents.push(...item._events)
  } catch (_) {}
})
```
The ?. swallows this without any error, warning, or observable symptom, flushDetached() still proceeds to write the events to disk and spawn the detached process, so the bug has no visible effect on its own. It only becomes a problem if this abort mechanism is relied on to actually cancel in-flight requests before next dev exits.

Expected behavior

this.queue should retain a reference to the Promise (or controller) that submitRecord() actually attaches _controller to, so that flushDetached()'s item._controller?.abort() genuinely aborts any in-flight telemetry request rather than silently no-op'ing.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: linux
  Arch: x64
  Version: #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Fri July 12 05:10:11 UTC 2026
  Available memory (MB): 12736
  Available CPU cores: 12
Binaries:
  Node: 20.20.2
  npm: 10.8.2
  Yarn: 1.22.22
  pnpm: N/A
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.3.0-canary.97
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.2.0
  react-dom: 19.2.0
  typescript: N/A
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Runtime

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next dev (local)

### Additional context

Found while investigating #96291. This is a separate, independent bug — it does not cause or contribute to the build hang described there, since next build uses Telemetry.flush(), which never reads _controller at all. This bug specifically affects flushDetached() (used by next dev's process-exit path), where the stored controller reference is always undefined.

open.title: next build can wait far beyond the built-in telemetry timeout when a caller signal is provided
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/cyhforlight/next-telemetry-timeout-repro

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the reproduction repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/cyhforlight/next-telemetry-timeout-repro.git
cd next-telemetry-timeout-repro
```

2. Build the Docker image:

```bash
docker build -t next-telemetry-timeout-repro .
```

3. Run the reproduction:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  --add-host telemetry.nextjs.org:127.0.0.1 \
  next-telemetry-timeout-repro
```

4. Observe that the telemetry-disabled build finishes normally, while the telemetry-enabled build takes significantly longer than the built-in five-second timeout.

The script prints `BUG REPRODUCED` and exits with code 0 when the telemetry-attributable delay exceeds the eight-second reproduction threshold.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

### Current behavior

The same unmodified project is built twice in the same container, with `.next` removed between runs. The only relevant difference is whether `NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1` is set.

With Next.js 16.2.6:

```text
telemetry disabled: 2.2s (exit 0)
telemetry enabled:  23.4s (exit 0)
attributable to telemetry: 21.2s
```

The telemetry request's built-in five-second timeout is not installed when the caller provides a signal. The production build path passes `postController.signal`, so a stalled request falls back to the HTTP client's substantially longer timeouts.

### Expected behavior

The caller-provided cancellation signal should not replace the telemetry request timeout. A stalled telemetry endpoint should stop delaying `next build` after approximately five seconds, while caller-initiated cancellation should continue to work.

open.title: Middleware Set-Cookie on prerendered static pages produces cacheable responses with s-maxage=31536000 - CDN caches and serves auth tokens to other users
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/uiYzzi/nextjs-middleware-setcookie-cache-leak

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the reproduction repo above
2. `npm install && npm run build && npm start`
3. Run the following curl command:

```bash
# Request 1: User A (has rt cookie, middleware sets Set-Cookie)
curl -sI -b "rt=USER_A" http://localhost:3000/
```

**Observed response:**
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
set-cookie: at=access_token_for_USER_A; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax
set-cookie: rt=refresh_token_for_USER_A; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax
x-nextjs-cache: HIT
x-nextjs-prerender: 1
Cache-Control: s-maxage=31536000
```

The response has **both** `Set-Cookie` (sensitive tokens) and `Cache-Control: s-maxage=31536000` (cacheable for 1 year).

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** When middleware adds `Set-Cookie` headers to a `NextResponse.next()` response for a prerendered (static) page, Next.js does not override the page's `Cache-Control: s-maxage=31536000` to `no-store`. The response contains both `Set-Cookie` and `s-maxage=31536000`.

**Expected:** When middleware adds `Set-Cookie` to a response, Next.js should set `Cache-Control: no-store` (or `private, no-cache`), because:
- RFC 6265 (HTTP State Management Mechanism) Section 7.3: shared caches must not store or distribute responses containing `Set-Cookie` headers to other clients, to prevent credential leakage
- A response with `Set-Cookie` contains user-specific data and is unsafe for shared CDN caching

### Provide environment information

```
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
Binaries:
  Node: 22.0.0
  npm: 10.0.0
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.2.12
  react: 19.1.0
  react-dom: 19.1.0
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

Also verified on Next.js 15.5.9 with the same result.

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Middleware, Cookies

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next start (local), Other (Deployed)

### Additional context

**Impact: Critical (Security)**

When deployed behind a non-Vercel CDN (e.g., AWS Amplify Hosting's managed CloudFront), this causes **cross-user authentication token leakage**: the CDN caches the response including `Set-Cookie` headers, and serves User A's tokens to User B on cache hits.

Vercel's [caching docs](https://vercel.com/docs/edge-network/caching) explicitly state that responses with `Set-Cookie` headers are NOT cached on Vercel's CDN. However, other CDNs (CloudFront, Cloudflare, Netlify) may cache responses with `Set-Cookie` when `s-maxage` is present, because the response explicitly declares itself cacheable.

This affects a very common pattern: BFF/OAuth architectures where middleware refreshes expired access tokens via `Set-Cookie`. Real-world incident: users were logged in as a different user they had never authenticated as.

**Suggested fix:** When `Set-Cookie` headers are present on a middleware `NextResponse.next()` response, automatically override `Cache-Control` to `no-store`:

```typescript
if (response.headers.has('set-cookie')) {
  response.headers.set('cache-control', 'no-store, must-revalidate');
}
```

Related issues:
- Amplify Hosting: https://github.com/aws-amplify/amplify-hosting/issues/4100
- Supabase similar incident: https://github.com/supabase/supabase-js/issues/1682
- Vercel CDN caching docs: https://vercel.com/docs/edge-network/caching
- RFC 6265 Section 7.3 (Cookie security): shared caches must not distribute responses with `Set-Cookie` to other clients

open.title: Dev server 500s on every request: concurrent getStaticPaths corrupts prerender-manifest.json
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/LouisTsang-jk/nextjs-prerender-manifest-race

### To Reproduce

```
1. git clone https://github.com/LouisTsang-jk/nextjs-prerender-manifest-race
2. npm install
3. ./repro.sh
```

`repro.sh` starts `next dev`, requests 10 pages under `app/[locale]/` concurrently, then checks `.next/dev/prerender-manifest.json` and issues one more request.

The app is minimal: a root `app/[locale]/layout.tsx` with `generateStaticParams` returning 9 locales, 10 trivial pages under it, and one route handler.

Since the failure is a race, a run can come back clean — rerunning hits it within the first couple of attempts on an M-series Mac. `race-unit.js` in the same repo reproduces the underlying read-modify-write deterministically (consistently ~180 corrupt manifests out of 300 rounds) with no Next.js involved.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** once two pages under the same dynamic segment resolve their static paths at the same time, `.next/dev/prerender-manifest.json` stops being valid JSON and **every subsequent request 500s**, including requests to completely unrelated routes:

```
⨯ SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input
    at JSON.parse (<anonymous>) {
  page: '/en/page-9'
}
 GET /en/page-9 500 in 4.9s
```

Two distinct corruption shapes show up, depending on how the writes interleave:

- `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input` — a read observes a file that is still being written.
- `SyntaxError: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON at position N` — valid JSON followed by leftover bytes.

From a real i18n app (9 locales, ~25 pages under `app/[locale]/`), the on-disk manifest after a collision was 1264 bytes with valid JSON only up to 1192:

```
..."previewModeEncryptionKey":"<64-hex value X>"}}ey":"<the same value X>"}}
                                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                              72 bytes left over from a previous, longer write
```

The trailing fragment repeats the *same* `previewModeEncryptionKey` as the valid portion, so both writes came from a single dev server process within one session — not stale cache, not two processes.

**Expected:** the manifest stays valid JSON regardless of how many pages resolve their static paths concurrently.

### Root cause

`packages/next/src/server/dev/next-dev-server.ts` (`getStaticPaths`) performs an unsynchronized read-modify-write on that file:

```ts
const rawExistingManifest = await fs.promises.readFile(
  pathJoin(this.distDir, PRERENDER_MANIFEST),
  'utf8'
)
const existingManifest: PrerenderManifest = JSON.parse(rawExistingManifest)
// ...mutate routes / dynamicRoutes...
const updatedManifest = JSON.stringify(existingManifest)

if (updatedManifest !== rawExistingManifest) {
  await fs.promises.writeFile(
    pathJoin(this.distDir, PRERENDER_MANIFEST),
    updatedManifest
  )
}
```

There is no lock, and the write is not atomic. Both `writeFile` calls open with `'w'` and write from offset 0, so when the shorter payload finishes last it only overwrites a prefix of the longer one and leaves the tail in place.

The blast radius comes from `base-server.ts` calling `getPrerenderManifest()` on every request (for `previewProps` and the `isSSG` check) — so one bad file takes down the whole dev server and the error surfaces on routes that have nothing to do with the pages that raced. In our case it consistently appeared on `/api/auth/session`, which sent us looking in entirely the wrong place.

> **Correction** (thanks to [@zoujimmy82-boop](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/96259#issuecomment-5128644737); verified on `canary`): the attribution above is wrong, though the user-visible effect is the same. `next-server.ts` memoizes into `_cachedPreviewManifest` and the dev server never overrides it, so it normally reads from disk once per process — but the assignment happens *after* `loadManifest()` returns, so while the file is corrupt the cache never populates and every request re-reads the bad file and re-throws. That is what makes it "every subsequent request", and why a later, longer write silently heals it. Of the two call sites cited, `previewProps` is in the constructor and the `isSSG` one goes through the memo. The path that keeps re-reading the file in dev is `route-modules/route-module.ts`, via `shouldCache: !this.isDev`.


A `generateStaticParams` on a root layout (the standard i18n setup) amplifies this: every page under `[locale]` runs its own read-modify-write cycle on first compile, so collision probability grows with page count. We only started seeing it regularly after crossing roughly 20 pages under `app/[locale]/`.

This is also why the failure looks intermittent and why `rm -rf .next` "sometimes helps": a later write whose payload is at least as long as the corrupt file silently repairs it, until the next collision.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 27.0.0: Mon Jun 29 21:25:16 PDT 2026; root:xnu-13432.0.50.501.3~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T8112
  Available memory (MB): 24576
  Available CPU cores: 8
Binaries:
  Node: 22.21.1
  npm: 10.9.4
  Yarn: N/A
  pnpm: 10.15.0
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.3.0-canary.97 // Latest available version is detected (16.3.0-canary.97).
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.2.0
  react-dom: 19.2.0
  typescript: 6.0.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Dynamic Routes, Internationalization (i18n)

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next dev (local)

### Additional context

Also reproduces on `16.2.7`. Not bundler specific — Turbopack and `--webpack` both hit it, since the code path is in the dev server rather than the bundler.

Workaround that does not require patching `node_modules` (included in the repro repo as `workaround-shim.cjs`) — makes writes to that one file atomic:

```jsonc
"dev": "NODE_OPTIONS='--require ./workaround-shim.cjs' next dev"
```

open.title: Turbopack dev server hangs all requests forever with sustained native CPU spin after its stdout pipe reader exits (`next dev | head -N`)
open.body:
### Verify canary release

- [x] I verified that the issue exists in the latest Next.js canary release (`16.3.0-canary.96`)

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/kando19804-oss/next-turbopack-broken-pipe-hang-repro

### To Reproduce

1. `pnpm install`
2. Start the dev server with an early-exiting stdout reader (bash / Git Bash):
   ```bash
   npx next dev -p 3111 2>&1 | head -15 &
   ```
3. Request the page repeatedly:
   ```bash
   for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -s -o /dev/null -m 10 -w "#$i -> %{http_code}\n" http://localhost:3111/; done
   ```

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** the server works normally for the first ~11 requests (~140 ms each), then — once its cumulative log output exceeds the pipe budget (the reader's `-N` lines + ~64 KB pipe buffer) — **every subsequent request hangs forever**:

```
#1  -> 200
...
#11 -> 200
#12 -> 000   (curl timeout)  ← hangs forever from here
#13 -> 000
...
```

While frozen (measured on the minimal repro):

- the process stays alive and keeps **LISTENing**; TCP connections are accepted but never answered (client sockets pile up in `CLOSE_WAIT`),
- **CPU time grows ~+26 s per 20 s wall clock (~1.3 cores) indefinitely while serving nothing**, memory grows slowly (530 → 567 MB in 20 s),
- a JS CPU profile (`--experimental-cpu-prof`, taken on a real app in the same state) shows the JS thread **99.9 % idle** — the stall and the CPU burn are on the native (Turbopack) side,
- the server never recovers; only killing the process helps.

**Control:** the identical server started with a file redirect instead of the pipe (`npx next dev -p 3111 > dev.log 2>&1`) served 1,000+ requests (cold start, 15-way parallel bursts, HMR churn) without a single failure.

**Expected:** anything but an unbounded silent hang + CPU spin. Either

- keep serving requests when stdout writes fail (drop log output), or
- fail fast with a visible error (e.g. exit on EPIPE).

### Provide environment information

```
Operating System:
  Platform: win32
  Arch: x64
  Version: Windows 11 Pro
  Available memory (MB): 65278
  Available CPU cores: 20
Binaries:
  Node: 20.20.1
  npm: 10.8.2
  pnpm: 10.32.1
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.2.11 (also reproduced on 16.3.0-canary.96)
  react: 19.2.3
  react-dom: 19.2.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A (repro), also reproduced with output: "standalone" on a large app
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Turbopack

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next dev (local)

### Additional context

- Real-world impact: piping a dev server's output through `head` to capture startup logs is common in CI scripts, tmux panes, and agent/automation harnesses (`pnpm dev 2>&1 | head -40 &`). On a large production app this exact pattern produced "the dev server dies after ~20–30 requests" with **no error output whatsoever** (stdout is gone), which took us two days and a CPU profile to trace back to the launch command. The freeze threshold scales with *log lines written*, not requests — a browser page that fires 15 API calls reaches it in one navigation, which made it look like an app bug.
- The repro's `next.config.js` sets `turbopack.root` only to keep workspace-root inference stable; it is unrelated.
- If the pipe budget is exhausted *during startup* (e.g. `| head -5`, smaller than the banner), the process dies before ever listening — the pathological hang + CPU spin happens when the budget is exhausted *after* startup.
- Reproduced on Windows 11 (pipe created by bash/Git Bash). The mechanism (writes to a broken/undrained stdout pipe stalling the native layer) is presumably platform-generic, but I could only verify on Windows.

open.title: App Router: chunk <script> tags get no fetchpriority and Chrome's LowPriorityAsyncScriptExecution delays their evaluation — hydration render storm (~30k commits) on cross-site assetPrefix CDNs
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/minsgiman/nextjs-hydration-livelock-repro

### To Reproduce

1. `npm install && npm run build && npm run start`
2. Launch Chrome (≥139) with the intervention forced onto same-origin scripts — this is exactly what **cross-site `assetPrefix` CDN** users get by default:
   `chrome --user-data-dir=/tmp/chrome-repro --enable-features="LowPriorityAsyncScriptExecution:low_pri_async_exec_cross_site_only/false"`
3. DevTools → Performance → CPU: 6× slowdown (approximates production-sized bundle parse/hydration cost).
4. Cold-navigate `about:blank` → `http://localhost:3000/` and measure `performance.getEntriesByType('navigation')[0]` → `loadEventStart - domContentLoadedEventEnd`.
5. Control run: same steps with `--disable-features=LowPriorityAsyncScriptExecution`.

Measured on the repro: **DCL→load ~119 ms vs ~4 ms** — the gap is purely chunk-**evaluation** delay (same-origin, downloads instant). On our production app (large bundle, ~29 chunk scripts) the delay reaches the intervention's full **1 s fallback timer**, and React streaming hydration amplifies it into a render storm: **~30,000 one-fiber commits, ~53k RunMicrotasks, ~106k FunctionCalls in ~1 s** on every cold navigation (Chrome trace: all chunks downloaded by ~110 ms; framework chunks evaluate ~150–175 ms; app chunks evaluate at ~1,148 ms — exactly when the commit storm ends). Verified causality in production both ways: `--disable-features=LowPriorityAsyncScriptExecution` eliminates the storm; forcing `cross_site_only/false` reproduces it on a same-site environment.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:**

1. App Router emits client/page chunks into the SSR HTML as parser-inserted `<script async>` **without `fetchpriority`**, and there is no config to add it (only `crossOrigin` is plumbed through to these tags; the flight stream also emits no `:H` preload/preinit hints for client-reference JS chunks — `serializeClientReference` writes only `:I` rows).
2. Chrome (M139+, default on desktop since Aug 2025 — ChromeOS later excluded, crbug.com/429069717; Android since Jan 2026) applies `LowPriorityAsyncScriptExecution` to cross-site async scripts, including these chunk tags: their evaluation task goes to a best-effort queue with a 1 s fallback (`PostTaskWithLowPriorityUntilTimeout` in `third_party/blink/renderer/core/script/script_runner.cc`). Chrome reads the priority from the ResourceRequest captured at fetch start (= HTML parse time), so **nothing can be done from client-side JS after the fact**.
3. During hydration, React (vendored `19.2.0-canary-0bdb9206-20250818`) does not park quietly on the blocked flight chunk: `handleThrow` classifies every `SuspenseException` as `SuspendedOnImmediate` (the `SuspendedOnData` quiet-wait branch is unreachable — never assigned in this build), each cycle commits a ~1-fiber tree and `scheduleRetryEffect` → `claimNextRetryLane` spawns a fresh retry lane that `markRootFinished` fails to suspend, so `ensureRootIsScheduled` re-arms via microtask + MessageChannel continuation. Both runaway guards are bypassed on this path (the "Maximum update depth" counter only counts Sync/InputContinuous/Default lanes; the shell-suspend guard requires a null suspense handler). The resulting loop saturates the main thread and **starves the very best-effort eval task it is waiting for** — a livelock until Chrome's 1 s timer force-runs the chunk. Note the bootstrap script itself escapes the intervention (React emits a `<link rel="preload" as="script" fetchpriority="low">` for it, and link-preloaded resources are exempt); the storm is driven by the preinit-emitted app/client chunks.

**Expected:**

- A supported way to opt these scripts out. Chrome explicitly excludes `fetchpriority="high"` scripts (`opt_out_high_fetch_priority_hint` defaults to `true`), so one attribute fully prevents the issue, e.g.:

```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  assetPrefix: 'https://cdn.example.com', // different registrable domain
  scriptFetchPriority: 'high', // applied to bootstrap/preinit/client chunk <script> tags
};
```

`crossOrigin` already demonstrates the plumbing for per-tag attributes, and React's `preinit`/`bootstrapScripts` APIs already accept `fetchPriority` — Next currently just doesn't pass one.

- Ideally, hydration should also degrade gracefully (quiet suspension instead of a retry storm) when a client chunk is downloaded but its evaluation is deferred by the browser.

### Provide environment information

```
Operating System: macOS (Darwin 24.6.0) (also reproduced on production traffic, desktop Chrome)
Binaries: Node 22.12.0, npm 10.x
Relevant Packages: next 15.5.18, react 19.1.0, react-dom 19.1.0 (App Router uses the vendored react-dom 19.2.0-canary-0bdb9206-20250818)
Browser: Chrome ≥ 139 (intervention default-on: desktop since Aug 2025 (ChromeOS later excluded) — https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/6636695; Android since Jan 2026 — https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7418954)
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Performance, Script (next/script), Runtime

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next start (local), Other (Deployed)

### Additional context

- Production evidence (controlled comparison, same code, only the CDN host's site relation differing): cross-site CDN → DCL→load ~1,000 ms / ~30,000 commits; same-site or same-origin → 1–30 ms / ~20–30 commits.
- Our current workaround is a custom-server streaming HTML transform that injects `fetchpriority="high"` into every `<script src=".../_next/static/chunks/...">` tag (plus a `document.head.appendChild` wrapper for late dynamically-inserted chunks). It fully resolves the issue but requires taking over compression and rewriting HTML — a heavy hammer for one attribute, and unavailable to `next start` users.
- Related: #77239 (triaged) — delayed client-chunk execution breaking selective hydration (FOUC variant). This report is the same root phenomenon amplified into a render livelock by the Chromium intervention.
- Chromium rollout: enabled by default on **desktop since M139 / Aug 2025** (ChromeOS later excluded — crbug.com/429069717) (https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/6636695), **Android since Jan 2026** (https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7418954) — which is why this regression appeared without any app deploy.
- Chromium references: feature defaults https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/common/features.cc (`low_pri_async_exec_*`), eligibility https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/script/classic_pending_script.cc

open.title: Bun runtime on Vercel: rewritten routes intermittently render the root page (HTTP 200)
open.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/tiagonrodrigues/nextjs-bun-runtime-rewrite-repro

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the reproduction. It is a bare App Router app: `next-intl` with
   `localePrefix: 'as-needed'`, a root page and three static child routes (`/alpha`, `/beta`,
   `/gamma`) that render nothing but their own name. No data fetching, no other dependencies.
2. Deploy it to Vercel. `vercel.json` contains `"bunVersion": "1.x"`, so it runs on the Bun runtime.
3. Run the included script against the deployment: `./check.sh https://<deployment>.vercel.app 40`

   It requests each unprefixed route and its locale-prefixed equivalent 40 times and compares the
   returned `<title>` with the one that route should render.
4. Remove `bunVersion` from `vercel.json`, redeploy, and run the same script for a control.

Because the failure rate is a fraction of requests, a handful of requests can easily come back
clean — run at least 40 iterations before concluding either way.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Expected:** `/alpha` always renders `app/[locale]/alpha/page.tsx`.

**Current:** a fraction of requests to the *unprefixed* routes return HTTP **200** carrying the
**root page's** HTML — `<title>ROOT PAGE</title>` in response to a request for `/alpha`.

Two deployments of the same code, differing only in `vercel.json`:

| Route | Bun runtime | Node runtime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/alpha` | **7 / 40 failed** | 0 / 40 |
| `/beta` | **4 / 40 failed** | 0 / 40 |
| `/gamma` | **7 / 40 failed** | 0 / 40 |
| `/pt/alpha` | 0 / 40 | 0 / 40 |
| `/pt/beta` | 0 / 40 | 0 / 40 |
| `/pt/gamma` | 0 / 40 | 0 / 40 |

Only the unprefixed default-locale routes fail. Those are the ones `localePrefix: 'as-needed'` has
to rewrite to `/[locale]/alpha?nxtPlocale=en`; `/pt/alpha` matches directly and never fails.

On a failing response the routing metadata is *correct* — `x-matched-path: /[locale]/alpha`, the
`hreflang` `link` headers and the `NEXT_LOCALE` cookie are all right. So the proxy ran and rewrote
correctly; what comes back is the wrong rendered module. The failure is downstream of the rewrite.

On a larger production app with the same setup, dynamic segments additionally return HTTP **500**
with this in the runtime logs:

```
Failed to handle /tours/sintra-tour?nxtPlocale=en&nxtPslug=sintra-tour ResolveMessage {}
```

`ResolveMessage` is Bun's module-resolution error type. I suspect the silent 200 and the 500 are
the same resolution failure landing differently, but I cannot prove that from the outside — the
200s leave no trace in the logs at all.

Does not reproduce locally under Bun: 300 requests against `bun run --bun next start`, including
concurrent bursts, all correct. It appears specific to the Bun runtime on Vercel Functions.

### Provide environment information

```
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
Binaries:
  Node: 25.2.1
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.2.10
  react: 19.2.4
  react-dom: 19.2.4
  typescript: 5.9.3
Other:
  next-intl: 4.8.1 (also reproduced on 4.13.4)
  Bun: vercel.json "bunVersion": "1.x"
  Deployment: Vercel Functions
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Runtime, Middleware, Routing (App Router)

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Vercel (Deployed)

### Additional context

This ran in production for a week on a site buying Google Ads before it was noticed, because the
200 variant is silent — it does not appear in error tracking, and the response carries the root
page's `<link rel="canonical">`.

Severity note: where responses are CDN-cacheable, a wrong response can get **cached**, and is then
served to *every* visitor of that URL until the entry expires. So the impact is not bounded by the
per-request failure rate.

Removing `bunVersion` fixed it across 24 projects; three sites where the rate had been quantified
went from 11-12%, ~12% and 8% to zero over 160, 135 and 60 requests respectively.

Previously filed as #96192, which was closed for missing a reproduction link and is locked, so I
could not add the reproduction there.
